beats.script_body: Manhattan’s 843-acre green oasis feels like nature, but very little here is natural. Every tree, every shrub, every lake, and most of the rolling hills were designed, planted, or blasted into existence by landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux back in the 1850s. The two took a two-and-a-half-mile tract of swampland, farms, and suburban towns and created an Arcadia that bore no resemblance to what came before. Underneath the park, 95 miles of drainage pipes were laid to fill and periodically empty the four man-made lakes; at ground level the site was transformed with six million bricks, 65,000 cubic tons of gravel, 26,000 trees, and 250,000 shrubs. Even the dirt was imported — the natural topsoil was so poor that 500,000 cubic feet of it was shipped in from New Jersey. As Olmsted wrote, “Every foot of the park, every tree and bush, every arch, roadway and walk, has been fixed where it is with a purpose.”

beats.source_passage: Manhattan’s 843-acre green oasis is the yin to the city’s neon, concrete, and office tower yang. Because, let’s face it, very little here is natural. Every tree, every shrub, every lake, and most of the rolling hills were designed, planted, or blasted into existence by landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux back in the 1850s, and their efforts still shape our experiences today. These two geniuses took a 21⁄2-mile tract of swampland, farms, and suburban towns and created an Arcadia that had no resemblance whatever to what had come before. Underneath the park, 95 miles of drainage pipes were installed, many to fill and periodically empty the four lakes that were created; at ground level the site was transformed using six million bricks, 65,000 cubic tons of gravel, 26,000 trees, and 250,000 shrubs. Even the dirt was imported; the natural topsoil was so poor that 500,000 cubic feet of topsoil was shipped in from New Jersey. As Olmsted once wrote, “Every foot of the park, every tree and bush, every arch, roadway and walk, has been fixed where it is with a purpose.”

fact_check.notes: 843 acres / Olmsted-Vaux 1850s / NJ topsoil corroborated by Olmsted Network and centralpark.com; figures (95 mi pipe, 6M bricks etc.) are Frommer's own and traceable to source.

beats.script_body: The park’s purpose was nothing less than the health of the city — a place where New Yorkers could blow off steam and escape the stresses of urban life. Olmsted wanted more: a park that would be a bridge between classes. “There need to be places and time for re-unions,” he wrote, “[where] the rich and the poor, the cultivated and the self-made, shall be attracted together and encouraged to assimilate.” It didn’t happen at first — the park was too far from the homes of poor New Yorkers for them to visit — but that ideal was realized once the city itself wrapped around the park, finally making it a true central park.

beats.source_passage: And what was that purpose? No less than the health of the city. Those who rallied for its creation felt that it was crucial to create a place where New Yorkers could blow off steam and get away from the stresses of urban life. Moreover, Olmsted wanted to create a park that would be a bridge between classes. “There need to be places and time for re-unions,” Olmsted wrote, “[where] the rich and the poor, the cultivated and the self-made, shall be attracted together and encouraged to assimilate.” Though that didn’t happen when the park was first finished—it was too far from the homes of poor New Yorkers for them to visit it—that ideal was realized when the city itself began to wrap around the park, making it finally a true central park.

beats.script_body: As you stroll, you’ll cross three deliberately different kinds of landscape. There are pastoral vistas like the Sheep Meadow, meant to evoke a cultivated countryside; primitive portions where dense forestation shuts out any view of the city; and promenade zones, once used by the city’s aristocracy as an extension of their parlors — a place to strut and be seen. There’s no right way to see the park; you can ignore any highlight list and simply wander its curving paths for hidden nooks and surprise vistas.

physical_cues.cue: Pastoral open meadows, dense forested zones, and formal promenade walkways around you

beats.source_passage: In your own strolls around the park, you’ll encounter three different types of landscapes: pastoral vistas such as the Sheep Meadow, which are meant to evoke a cultivated countryside; primitive portions where dense forestation shuts out any view of the city; and promenade zones, which were once used by the city’s aristocracy as an extension of their parlors, a place to strut and be seen. I’ve created a brief list of highlights that includes all three, but feel free to ignore the list altogether and just wander the curving paths of the park, exploring its hidden nooks, surprise vistas, ball fields, and playgrounds. There’s no right way to see or do this park.

beats.script_body: This turreted castle is Olmsted and Vaux’s “folly” — a fantasy building — and it sits atop the second-highest elevation in the park. Inside is a nature observatory with good rainy-day activities for children. From Belvedere you also look down on the Great Lawn, which has gone through a number of incarnations: first a reservoir, then in the 1930s “Hooverville,” the shantytown where hundreds of homeless families lived out the Depression. Today it’s laid out in ballfields and often used as a concert space — Simon and Garfunkel famously reunited here in the 1980s in a widely televised concert.

beats.script_body: In front of the castle is the Delacorte Theater, where the famed Shakespeare in the Park is performed — a star-studded and free evening of theater staged only in the summer months. If you decide to take in a show, know that you could end up spending four or more hours standing on line for tickets. They’re passed out at 1pm in front of the theater, but depending on the show’s popularity, crowds generally show up hours before that, and some even camp overnight at the gate to the park.

beats.script_body: This Victorian spinner is most children’s favorite stop in the park. It’s not the original — the first burned down in the 1950s — but it’s a beaut, built on Coney Island in 1908 and featuring some of the tallest merry-go-round horses in the U.S. It’s also far more humane than the original carousel, which was rotated by a blind mule and a horse toiling away in the basement.

beats.script_body: Because of its small size, this zoo is at its best showing off smaller animals. The indoor, multilevel Tropic Zone is a real highlight — a steamy rainforest home to everything from black-and-white colobus monkeys to emerald tree boa constrictors to a leaf-cutter ant farm, plus a very cool poison-dart-frog exhibit. The large penguin enclosure in the Polar Circle is better than the one at San Diego’s SeaWorld. For the littlest visitors, the nearby Tisch Children’s Zoo has goats, llamas, and potbellied pigs in a petting-zoo playground.

beats.source_passage: Because of its small size, the zoo is at its best with its displays of smaller animals. So is the large penguin enclosure in the Polar Circle, which is better than the one at San Diego’s SeaWorld. For the littlest ones, the nearby Tisch Children’s Zoo has goats, llamas, potbellied pigs, and more in a petting zoo and playground that’s a real blast for the 5-and-under set.

beats.script_body: This handsome obelisk was a gift to the United States from Egypt in 1881, in recognition of the help this country gave in building the Suez Canal. Transporting the 200-ton pillar took 38 days by ship from Alexandria to New York — and then another 144 days just to haul it from the Hudson River into Central Park. It originally stood at the Temple of the Sun in Heliopolis, believed to have been erected in 1600 b.c.; the Romans moved it in the 12th century to the front of a temple built by Cleopatra, which is how it got its name. A plaque at the base translates the hieroglyphics.

beats.script_body: Bethesda Terrace is, without a doubt, the architectural heart of the park, and you’re likely to see a bride or two using this lovely area as a backdrop for wedding photographs. Approaching from the Mall, you’ll reach two massive posts on either side of the stairs, carved with symbols for day and night — the side with the witch on a broom is “night.” Look, too, at the carvings on the stairs down to the fountain: they represent the four seasons, and no two are alike.

beats.source_passage: At the uptown end of the mall (just across the road), Bethesda Terrace is, without a doubt, the architectural heart of the park. You’re likely to see a bride or two here, as many use this extraordinarily lovely area as a backdrop for wedding photographs. If you approach it from the Mall, you’ll come to two massive posts on either side of the stairs, carved with symbols representing day and night (the side with the witch on a broom is “night”). Take a look as well at the carvings on the stairs down to the fountain area; they represent the four seasons, and no two are alike.

beats.script_body: Bethesda Fountain commemorates the opening of the Croton Aqueduct, which finally solved New York’s water problems in 1842; the fountain itself was finished in 1864. It was sculpted by Emma Stebbins, the first woman to receive this type of commission from the city. Her statue represents the angel Bethesda, who blesses the water with one hand while carrying a lily — the symbol of purity — in the other.

beats.script_body: In their original plans, Olmsted and Vaux called this area the “Promenade” and intended it as an “open air hall of reception.” Today the grand, elm–lined walkway is bedecked with statues; at its uptown end is an underused band shell, and just west of that is one of the park’s premier party spots — an unofficial rollerblading rink where regulars dance-skate for hours each weekend to blasting disco music. It’s quite a scene.

beats.script_body: At the southernmost tip of Manhattan, Battery Park has been growing kudzu-like for decades — it’s now a string of eclectic park spaces hugging the waterfront from just above the original Battery Park, where the Statue of Liberty ferry terminal sits, all the way up to Chambers Street, 21 acres in all. At the downtown-most end are stirring war monuments and the Seaglass Carousel, which dips and swoops riders around on massive plexiglass fish. Walking uptown you’ll find expansive lawns, a riverside promenade, terrific playgrounds, and a yacht marina.

beats.script_body: Just behind the New York Public Library, this park is a welcome respite from the endless high-rises and crushing crowds of midtown — a 4-acre lawn surrounded by benches, statuary, and London planetree–shaded promenades, much like the Tuileries Gardens in Paris. It’s notable for its extensive programs of public concerts, movies, and even free juggling classes every good-weather day at noon. From roughly May through October the Sixth Avenue end becomes a stage for Broadway performers and free summer movies; in winter a small pond is set up for free ice-skating.

beats.script_body: Who knew “adaptive reuse” could be this sexy? Domino Park sits on riverside property once owned by the Domino Sugar Refinery. In adapting the land, designer Lisa Switkin — of the firm behind the High Line — protected the landmarked refinery, making the hulking factory a spooky centerpiece, and reused other industrial artifacts to wonderful effect. That includes a gantry, a massive platform holding two cranes, painted the same turquoise that once lined the refinery’s walls; it’s now an elevated walkway with spectacular Manhattan views. In front of it sits a playground built to look like a mini-refinery, a volleyball court flanked by old syrup tanks, and a grove of metal corkscrews once used to stir syrup.

The only private park on this list (but open to the public), Domino Park sits on a quarter acre of riverside property once owned by the Domino Sugar Refinery. In adapting the land, designer Lisa Switkin (of the firm behind the High Line; see p. 262) protected that landmarked structure, making the hulking factory a spooky centerpiece of the park, and re-using other industrial artifacts found here to wonderful effect. That includes a gantry, basically a massive platform that holds two cranes, painted the same shade of turquoise that once lined the refinery’s walls; it’s now an elevated walkway affording spectacular Manhattan views. In front of it is a playground that looks like a minirefinery, a volleyball court flanked by old syrup tanks, and a grove of metal corkscrews the height of family Christmas trees (they were once used to stir syrup).

beats.script_body: Situated a half-mile south of Manhattan, the 172-acre Governors Island was for many years a Coast Guard installation. Before that it was an army post for nearly 200 years and played a part in the Revolutionary War. In April 2010, New York City took it over. Because it had been a military base for so long, few New Yorkers — much less tourists — had ever visited. That has changed: much of the island is now a public park, with 22 acres designated a national monument centered around two 1812-era fortresses. In 2016, new parkland crowned by four man-made hills opened, giving visitors even more stellar views of Manhattan.

beats.script_body: For years a secret, untamed garden hovered above the cityscape of Chelsea and Hell’s Kitchen. Formed from wild grass, flower, and weed seeds that randomly blew onto the tracks of a mile-and-a-half abandoned elevated railway, it became a hidden-in-plain-sight oasis for those New Yorkers brave and limber enough to scale the trestles. When the city began planning to tear down the historic rail structure — constructed 1929 to 1934 — a movement was born to save it and turn it into a grand public promenade with easy access from the street. Opened in 2009, it’s beautifully landscaped, in many places with the very “weeds” that once grew there, replanted where they wouldn’t crowd out the rest.

There’s also a free skate park and a minigolf course.

beats.script_body: Gotham’s newest park seems to float like a watery mirage in the Hudson River. The engineering and architecture by Thomas Featherwick — the designer of Vessel — is stupendous: a set of 132 concrete “tulips,” all of differing heights, emerge from the water and join to form the base of the isle. On top of that Seuss-like structure are hills, amphitheaters, and eateries linked by winding paths and boulder scrambles. Landscaper Signe Nielson spared no expense, reportedly spending $5 million to cover the island with some 35 species of trees and 270 varieties of perennials, grasses, and bulbs, many chosen to attract bees and birds. It’s a gift to the city from media mogul Barry Diller, who spent $260 million on its construction.

beats.source_passage: Gotham’s newest park seems to float like a watery mirage in the Hudson River. The engineering and architecture by Thomas Featherwick (of Vessel; see p. 199) is stupendous, with a set of 132 concrete “tulips,” all of differing heights, emerging from the water and connecting to form the base of the isle. On top of that Seuss-like structure, hills were built, and amphitheaters, and eateries, all connected by a network of sinuously winding paths, stairs, and boulder scrambles. Landscaping superstar Signe Nielson was in charge of the greenery, and she spared no expense—it’s been reported she spent $5 million to cover the island with some 35 species of trees, 65 species of shrubs, and 270 varieties of perennials, grasses, vines, and bulbs. Many were chosen for their appeal to bees and birds, as it’s hoped this will be a sanctuary for those critters. It’s a gift to the city from media mogul Barry Diller, who spent $260 million for its construction and has pledged to supply money for its upkeep into the foreseeable future.

beats.script_body: Also known as Jeffrey’s Hook Lighthouse, this historic beauty sits under the George Washington Bridge in Fort Washington Park, and it inspired the 1942 children’s classic The Little Red Lighthouse and the Great Gray Bridge by Hildegarde Swift and Lynd Ward. Built in New Jersey in 1880, it was reconstructed and moved to this spot in 1921 and stayed operational until 1947. It was slated for removal in 1951, but a public outcry over its popularity saved it; it’s now a New York City landmark and on the National Register of Historic Places.

beats.script_body: Designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux after their success with Central Park, this 562-acre expanse of woodland, meadows, and ponds is considered by many to be their masterpiece and the pièce de résistance of Brooklyn. The best approach is from Grand Army Plaza, presided over by the monumental Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Memorial Arch of 1892, honoring Union veterans. For the finest view of the lush landscape, follow the path to Meadowport Arch and on through to the Long Meadow, taking the loop around it — about an hour’s walk.

beats.script_body: Another masterwork by Olmsted and Vaux, Riverside Park has always had one advantage over Central Park: glorious river views, which its garden-laced promenades make the most of. Among its monuments is Grant’s Tomb at 122nd Street, the largest mausoleum in the United States at 8,100 square feet. And the answer to that old riddle — who’s buried in Grant’s tomb? — is: no one. Ulysses S. Grant and his wife aren’t buried at all; their sarcophagi lie above ground.

beats.script_body: This is the city’s funkiest green space, and it’s seen its share of political protest. In 1988, a standoff between the police and the homeless people living here culminated in five days of rioting and charges of police brutality. Incorporated as a park in 1878, Tompkins Square once had a band shell where an early version of the Grateful Dead made their East Coast debut, though that has since been torn down.

beats.script_body: Union Square Park’s tradition of political activism goes back to the very first Labor Day Parade in 1882, which ended right here. Ever since, it’s been soapbox central — a place where orators come daily to blast whatever administration is in power and weigh in on the big topics of the day. A statue of Gandhi, a gift of the Indian people, calmly watches over the proceedings, a fresh wreath of flowers always draped about his neck.
